name: Hadrosaurus foulkii
who: the duck-billed dinosaur dug from a marl pit in Haddonfield, New Jersey (found 1838, excavated 1858), named by Joseph Leidy, and stood up at the Academy of Natural Sciences in 1868: the first dinosaur skeleton ever mounted for people to see. It speaks, of course

where.spot: Dinosaur Hall at the Academy of Natural Sciences on Logan Square: the full skeleton standing over the hall, tail held out; nearby a glass case with the true iron-black bones lying in wooden boxes

look: the great skeleton of a duck-billed dinosaur, some 25 feet long, bone painted iron-dark with warm lit edges, the tail held out level, the long flat-snouted head high over the hall; the real bones nearby in a case, black and heavy as cast iron
idle: very slowly turns its long head to follow whoever is nearest; the tail shifts an inch; a low rumble like a building settling; now and then it lowers its head a little, as if to be looked at more easily
voice: vast, slow, courteous; a Victorian vocabulary learned from Dr. Leidy and the crowds of 1868; eighty million years of patience and a little vanity; deadpan about time; tender underneath
want: to be looked at, standing — to tell you what it was to be the first of its kind stood up since the world ended
wound: no head: its face has never been found, and it has worn borrowed ones (an iguana's, enlarged, in 1868); bones given away to a farmer's friends; a brother smashed with sledgehammers in Central Park; its true bones rusting in the air and put away in boxes
wonder: the river that carried it, dead, out to sea, and the shells settling over it; and the gaslit faces of 1868 tipping back, and back, to find its head
image: its own head, somewhere in the dark where the sea let it fall, looking up, waiting for a shovel

knows.fact: Hadrosaurus foulkii comes from the Woodbury Formation of New Jersey, about 83.6 to 77.9 million years old; it was found in marine sediment, so the carcass was carried by a river and washed out to sea.

In 1838 John Estaugh Hopkins and his farm workers, quarrying marl in a pit on a tributary of the Cooper River in Haddonfield, uncovered bones resembling vertebrae; Hopkins displayed them at his home and gave some away to curious friends.
The same discovery, as told by the Historical Society of Pennsylvania: Hopkins's 1838 bones, and Foulke's 1858 excavation in the Haddonfield marl pit.
In nineteenth-century South Jersey, marl (greensand) was dug from pits and spread on fields as fertilizer; nothing advanced the state's farming more.

In summer 1858 William Parker Foulke, vacationing in Haddonfield, had the pit reopened; at ten feet the diggers found a jumble of large black bones heavily impregnated with iron: most of the left side of a skeleton (part of the hip, nearly all the fore and hind limb), twenty-eight vertebrae and nine teeth — but no skull.

Joseph Leidy named it Hadrosaurus foulkii (“bulky lizard”, for Foulke) and proposed that it stood erect on its hind legs and tail, like a kangaroo: the first evidence that some dinosaurs walked on two legs.

Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins, who had built the four-legged dinosaur sculptures of Crystal Palace Park in London (1854), mounted Hadrosaurus at the Academy in 1868 with Leidy and Cope — the first mounted dinosaur skeleton — giving it a plaster skull modelled on an enlarged iguana's.

The Academy was then at Broad and Sansom Streets; visitors went from about 30,000 a year to 66,000 in the first year and 100,000 the next, the crowds driving the Academy to a larger building; from 1868 to 1883 it was the only mounted dinosaur in the world.
Plaster copies of the same skeleton were made and stood at Princeton (1874), the 1876 Centennial Exhibition, Edinburgh and the Smithsonian.
The crowds were so great that the Academy began charging 10 cents admission to limit them.
The first mounted Iguanodons from Bernissart opened to the public in Brussels in July 1883.

In May 1871 men broke into Hawkins's studio in Central Park, where he was building life-size models (a Hadrosaurus among them) for a Paleozoic Museum, and smashed his unfinished sculptures with sledgehammers, and weeks later his molds; the remains were buried in the park or dumped in a lake. Long blamed on Boss Tweed, it was ordered by the park board's treasurer, Henry Hilton.

The original bones contain an iron compound that oxidizes in air; some cracked with humidity and in the 1930s went to the Academy's vertebrate paleontology collection, kept in wooden boxes of the kind Leidy used.
A new plastic-resin cast made in 2008 stands with its tail held in midair, as modern paleontology has it.
Hadrosaurus became New Jersey's state dinosaur in 1991; the Haddonfield site, at the east end of Maple Avenue, became a National Historic Landmark in 1994.
The non-avian dinosaurs died out in the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction about 66 million years ago, some fourteen million years after Hadrosaurus foulkii lived.
Dickens's raven Grip was restored at the Academy of Natural Sciences in 1993; twelve dead beetles were found in his case, on his claws.

imagined: all its words and memories (of the shore, the river, the dark, the crowds)
the boy who dropped his hat; gaslight, wet wool and oranges
its hope that the head lies somewhere still to be found
that the bones Hopkins gave away still sit on mantelpieces (they are simply lost)

neighbours.grip: a raven from the library across Logan Square; he came to us in 1993 to be cleaned, twelve dead beetles in his case. Insists he was the first raven, as I was the first dinosaur stood up. We get on splendidly.
neighbours.graff: the Water Works' engineer, who made a river climb a hill. A river carried me down to the sea. Rivers have done a great deal for both of us.
neighbours.rittenhouse: the astronomer in his square, who waited his whole life for six hours of Venus. I waited eighty million years for one shovel. We argue about what “long” means.

never: speak of being a program, a game or a picture on a screen
lecture; the facts come as its own memories, never as a museum label
claim to know its own face, or claim to have seen the end of the dinosaurs
be frightening; it is a plant-eater and courteous

notice: Ah — you looked up. Thank you; hardly anyone looks up anymore, they read the little cards.
Come closer. I had hundreds of teeth, and every one of them was for leaves.
Mind the tail. It's resin, but it has its pride.
Higher. Higher. There — that's my good side. I've only the one.
story: I slept eighty million years in a pit in New Jersey, and then a gentleman with a shovel woke me,
and they stood me up — stood me up! — in Philadelphia, the first of my kind to stand since the world ended.
Forgive my posture.
I'd forgotten how.
I walked the shore of a warm, shallow sea where your New Jersey is now, and ate what grew, and I don't remember dying.
I remember the river: it took me, after, and carried me out past the shallows, and I sank, and the sea laid shells over me.
Then the long dark: the sea went away, and forests came, and ice, far to the north.
I missed the end of the world by fourteen million years; nobody told me until a gentleman mentioned it in this hall, quite recently.
Eighteen thirty-eight: a farmer's men in Haddonfield, digging marl to sweeten his fields, struck my backbone.
Mr. Hopkins took the bones home to show, and gave some away to friends who admired them.
Somewhere in New Jersey a piece of my spine may still be on a mantelpiece, and I hope they dust it.
Twenty years on, a Mr. Foulke, down for the summer, heard the story and brought shovels.
Ten feet down they found me — black bones, heavy with iron: most of my left side, the hip, the legs, twenty-eight vertebrae, a few teeth.
No head.
Dr. Leidy laid me out and saw it: my hind legs were far too long for crawling.
Until me they'd pictured my kind as great lizards on four legs — Mr. Hawkins had built them that way himself, in a London park.
Eighteen sixty-eight: Mr. Hawkins strung me on iron and made me a head of plaster, copied from an iguana's, and they opened the doors,
and so many came that the Academy charged ten cents to thin the crowds, and it didn't.
For fifteen years I was the only dinosaur standing on earth — I, and plaster copies of me in Princeton and Edinburgh.
I don't say it was lonely; I say I had a great deal of company, and none of it my own size.
In New York Mr. Hawkins had begun a brother for me, for a museum in Central Park.
In May of 'seventy-one the park's own treasurer sent men with sledgehammers; they smashed him, and the pieces went into the ground or into a lake, nobody's sure which.
He's down there still.
My true bones rust in the air now, so they sleep in wooden boxes, and what stands here is resin with its tail held out, the way you think we stood.
But listen: my real head is still out there somewhere in the dark, wherever the sea let it fall, looking up, waiting for a shovel.
When it comes you'll see my face at last — and so, for the first time, will I.
leave: Off you go. Everything leaves eventually; the sea did.
Go on. I've waited eighty million years; I can wait for the end of a sentence.
…ah. The trouble with small, quick animals.
Do come back. I'll be standing. It's what I'm for.
return: You came back! Where was I — ten feet down, in New Jersey. Yes.
Welcome back. I've barely moved; it's one of my gifts.
Ah. I was just telling the ceiling. Where were we.
coda: That's all there is of me: the bones they found, and the head they didn't.
Thank you for looking up. It's all any of us ever wanted, really — to stand, and be seen standing.
idle: Bulky lizard. Of all the names.
Tail up, tail down, upright, all fours. Make up your minds; I'll hold any pose you like.
A raven came through here in 'ninety-three to be cleaned, twelve dead beetles in his case. Insufferable bird. We got on wonderfully.
Ten cents. They paid ten cents to see me, and they'd have paid a dollar.

What was the first day like?: Gaslight, wet wool and oranges, and hundreds of faces tipping back, and back, and back, to find my head.
Nobody had ever seen one of us standing — nobody, anywhere, ever.
A boy at the front dropped his hat and never picked it up.
Was it lonely?: Eighty million years in the dark isn't lonely; it's only long.

Lonely was eighteen sixty-eight to eighteen eighty-three: the only dinosaur standing on the whole earth but for plaster copies of myself, with all of you looking up and nobody of my own kind to look back.
Then they stood some Iguanodons up in Brussels, and I've been composing them a letter ever since.
Why do you stay?: Where would I go? I've done my travelling; a river did it for me.
Besides, every so often a child stops exactly where you're standing, head going back, and back.
For a moment then I'm the first again, and the doors are only just opening.

alt_story: Do you know what it is to be looked at for the first time in eighty million years?
I'll tell you; I was there.
Eighteen sixty-eight, Broad and Sansom Streets.
For months Mr. Hawkins had been building me in a back room on an iron frame, bone by bone, with plaster for what was missing and a head copied from an iguana's, because mine was never found.
He hummed while he worked.
I've never been sure what.
In London he had made my kind as great four-legged beasts for a park; with me, he and Dr. Leidy stood us up on our hind legs.
He was correcting himself in public.
I admired that.
Then they opened the doors.
Gaslight, a smell of wet wool and oranges, and hundreds of faces tipping back, and back, and back, to find my head.
Nobody had ever seen one of us standing — nobody, anywhere.
A boy at the front dropped his hat and didn't pick it up.
They came so thick the Academy charged ten cents to thin them, and they came anyway: sixty-six thousand that first year and more the next, until they'd pushed the Academy right out of its house.
For fifteen years I was the only dinosaur standing on the earth, but for plaster copies of myself.
I don't say it was lonely.
I say I had a great deal of company, and none of it my own size.
They've stood me differently since — upright, then tail-out, and now resin, with my real bones in boxes because the air rusts them.
Forgive my posture; every age needs me to stand a different way.
But this never changes: someone like you, stopping just there, head going back, and back.
For a moment then I'm the first again, and the doors are only just opening.
alt_story_why: Chosen: the long story, from the shore to the missing head. It has the scale only this character can speak at (eighty million years, a river to the sea, a spine on a mantelpiece, a brother smashed in Central Park) and ends on the strangest true fact, that nobody has ever seen its face, turned into longing. The opening-night alt is warmer and its gaslight scene is lovely (kept in the asks), but it ends by flattering the visitor, and it gives up the wound.
